lede: The same days told from Constance and from Prague. The pairs will be added as the modules are carried.

pairs.frage: The haycart, told by Hus's friend and by a citizen of Constance.
pairs.note: Mladoňovice, who was there with Hus's protector, calls the haycart story a false rumour: a cart went out for hay with its cover on, and people talked. Richental tells it as fact, with a flask of wine and a white loaf, and has a Bohemian knight ask Hus why he broke his own safe conduct. If Hus fled, the king's promise no longer bound anyone; the story mattered for exactly that reason.

pairs.frage: The council's letter to the barons of Bohemia, and the barons' answer five weeks later.
pairs.note: The council writes that Hus was heard many times, in public and before the king, that he confessed absurd beliefs and was convicted of open heresy, and that it tried in charity to save him. The lords answer that he was condemned 'not confessed, nor lawfully convicted', on the word of the kingdom's enemies. Both speak the language of procedure; the question between them was whether refusing to abjure what one denies having taught is obstinacy.

pairs.frage: Hus defended by the lords of Bohemia in September 1415, and by Jerome before the council in May 1416.
pairs.note: The lords call Hus 'a man good, just and catholic', who taught nothing against the faith; Jerome, as Poggio reports him, calls Hus 'a good, just and holy man' who spoke not against the Church but against the abuses, pride and pomp of the clergy. Whether Jerome knew the lords' letter, the sources do not say. The council, which had been sent the letter and had heard Jerome, condemned him within the week.

pairs.frage: Sigismund in the lords' letter of September 1415, and in Prague in July 1420.
pairs.note: In 1415 the lords of Bohemia excepted one man from their curse on all who called Bohemia heretical: Sigismund, 'our heir and lord to come, whom we believe and hope to be innocent'. Five years later the heir came with a crusade, was crowned in the castle without the city, and was cursed by his own army as a patron of heretics. Between the two texts lie the safe conduct, the sentence and the death of Wenceslas; this is the second half of the site's thesis.
